theory.title: DNS: The Internet's Phone Book
theory.recap: Last level DHCP gave you a source IP so routers would accept you. This level you have a source IP, but your destination is a name, not an address. Routers cannot match names - you need DNS to translate first, then it's longest-prefix match all over again.
theory.plainObjective: You know your destination by name but not by address. Visit the DNS resolver first to get the IP, then route through R1 using longest-prefix match.
theory.summary: DNS is the first thing that happens when you visit any website. Before a single byte of content loads, your device asks a DNS resolver for the IP behind the domain name - exactly what you just did.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Names vs addresses
bodyParagraphs.text: Humans remember names like web.fcc. Routers forward packets using IP addresses like 10.0.2.30. DNS (Domain Name System) bridges that gap by translating names to IPs.

bodyParagraphs.heading: The A record
bodyParagraphs.text: A DNS A record maps one domain name to one IPv4 address. When your browser loads a website, the first thing it does is ask a DNS resolver for the A record of that domain. Only then does it know where to send the packet.

bodyParagraphs.heading: What happens without DNS?
bodyParagraphs.text: Routers cannot forward traffic without a destination IP. If you skip the DNS resolver and head straight to R1, the routing table has nothing to match against. You must resolve the name first.

bodyParagraphs.heading: After DNS - longest-prefix match
bodyParagraphs.text: Once DNS resolves the name to 10.0.2.30, R1's table has three overlapping rows that all touch it. Pick the most specific one - the rule you learned in The Subnet Maze.

theory.mission:
Your destination is the name web.fcc. Resolve it at the DNS server, then at R1 pick the most specific route to the resolved address.

Three routes will match. Only one is the right answer.

termIntroductions.headline: Domain Name
termIntroductions.body: Instead of memorising 10.0.2.30, you use the name web.fcc. A domain name is a human-readable label assigned to an IP address. Your packet knows its destination by name but needs the actual IP before it can be routed.

termIntroductions.headline: DNS - Domain Name System
termIntroductions.body: DNS is a distributed database that maps domain names to IP addresses. When you visit a website, your device queries a DNS resolver before sending any other traffic. The resolver looks up the name and returns the IP.

termIntroductions.headline: A Record
termIntroductions.body: An A record (Address record) is the most common DNS record type. It maps a domain name to an IPv4 address. web.fcc -> 10.0.2.30. Your routing table can now match that IP and forward the packet correctly.
